specStatements.text: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols.
Students should be able to draw and interpret circuit diagrams.
For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.
Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge. Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation:
charge flow = current × time
[Q = I t]
charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
time, t, in seconds, s
A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop.

The current (I) through a component depends on both the resistance (R) of the component and the potential difference (V) across the component. The greater the resistance of the component the smaller the current for a given potential difference (pd) across the component.
Questions will be set using the term potential difference. Students will gain credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage.
Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation:
potential difference = current × resistance
[V = I R]
potential difference, V, in volts, V
current, I, in amperes, A (amp is acceptable for ampere)
resistance, R, in ohms, Ω
Required practical activity 3:
Use circuit diagrams to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. This should include:
• the length of a wire at constant temperature
• combinations of resistors in series and parallel.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
Students should be able to explain that, for some resistors, the value of R remains constant but that in others it can change as the current changes.

The current through an ohmic conductor (at a constant temperature) is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor. This means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes.
The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component.
The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases.
The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.
The applications of thermistors in circuits eg a thermostat is required.
The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.
The application of LDRs in circuits eg switching lights on when it gets dark is required.
Students should be able to:
• explain the design and use of a circuit to measure the resistance of a component by measuring the current through, and potential difference across, the component
• draw an appropriate circuit diagram using correct circuit symbols.
Students should be able to use graphs to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear and relate the curves produced to the ir function and properties.

Required practical activity 4: use circuit diagrams to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 6 and 7.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: Questions will be set using the term potential difference. Students will gain credit for the correct use of either potential difference or voltage.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every stem, concept definition and correct option in this material sets the quantity using the term potential difference, abbreviated pd exactly as the specification abbreviates it. The word voltage is never used to pose a question, so a student who has only met the term potential difference is never disadvantaged. Where students' own wording is discussed, it is stated explicitly that voltage is an acceptable alternative and earns credit, so nobody is taught that voltage is wrong. The symbol is always V and the unit always volts, V, as the specification gives them. This boundary statement therefore carries no questions of its own.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 6 and 7.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This is a mapping note for teachers, listing which apparatus and techniques skills Required practical activity 3 develops. It states no physics that a student can be assessed on, so it is honoured by treating it as teacher-facing: no question asks a student to recite AT numbers, or to say which AT skills a practical covers. The underlying skills themselves — assembling circuits from a diagram, using ammeters and voltmeters, and measuring lengths of wire — are assessed through the practical questions on statements S19 to S22.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This is a cross-reference to another part of the specification document rather than examinable physics. It is honoured by not manufacturing questions about working scientifically statements or maths skill codes, and by not asking students to reproduce the contents of the Key opportunities for skills development section. The mathematical demand it points to — rearranging V = I R and Q = I t, converting minutes to seconds, and reading I–V graphs — is exercised inside the ordinary content questions instead.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: As with sn02, this is a teacher-facing mapping of Required practical activity 4 onto the apparatus and techniques list. No question asks which AT skills are covered, or what AT 6 and AT 7 are. The skills are exercised implicitly instead: the questions on statement S38 ask about constructing the circuit and about holding the resistor at constant temperature, which is the practical substance those AT codes describe.

concepts.definition: Circuit diagrams use standard symbols, so that any circuit can be read by anyone. The symbols needed are: open switch, closed switch, cell, battery, diode, resistor, variable resistor, LED, lamp, fuse, voltmeter, ammeter, thermistor and LDR. A cell is one long thin line beside one short thick line; a battery is two or more cells drawn in line. A resistor is a plain rectangle; a variable resistor is that rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it. An ammeter is a circle containing A; a voltmeter is a circle containing V.

To draw a circuit diagram, components are joined by straight lines standing for connecting wires, with each component shown by its correct standard symbol. To interpret one, trace the loops: components on the same single loop are in series and carry the same current, while components on separate branches are in parallel. An ammeter is always drawn in the loop with the component whose current is being measured; a voltmeter is always drawn as a separate branch across the component.

For electrical charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference, such as a cell, a battery or a power supply. A complete loop on its own is not enough: with nothing to push the charges round, the current is zero. The source does not create the charges — they are already in the metal — it provides the potential difference that makes them drift one way.

Electric current is a flow of electrical charge. The size of the electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, how much charge passes a point each second. It is not a flow of energy, and it is not the speed of the individual electrons, which drift very slowly even when the current is large.

concepts.term: Charge flow equation Q = I t
concepts.definition: Charge flow, current and time are linked by the equation charge flow = current × time, written [Q = I t]. Rearranged, I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I. The time must be in seconds before it is substituted, so minutes and hours have to be converted first: 5.0 minutes is 300 s.
Charge flow, Q, is measured in coulombs, C. The coulomb is a quantity of charge, not a rate: one coulomb passes a point when a current of one ampere flows for one second.

Current, I, is measured in amperes, A; amp is acceptable for ampere. One ampere is a flow of one coulomb of charge each second, so the ampere measures a rate of flow of charge while the coulomb measures an amount of charge.

Time, t, is measured in seconds, s. Because the equations of this section are defined with time in seconds, any time given in minutes or hours must be converted before substitution: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600.

concepts.term: Current in a single closed loop
concepts.definition: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop. Charge is not used up as it goes round, so an ammeter placed anywhere in that loop gives the same reading, whether it is before, between or after the components. What the components use is energy, not charge.

The current through a component depends on both the resistance of the component and the potential difference across it. Resistance opposes the flow of charge: the greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it. The current can therefore be changed either by changing the pd or by changing the resistance.

Potential difference, V, is measured in volts, V. It is the quantity that drives charge round a circuit, and it is measured across a component rather than through it. Questions are set using the term potential difference; a student who writes voltage instead gains credit, because voltage is an accepted alternative name for the same quantity.

Current, potential difference or resistance can be calculated using the equation potential difference = current × resistance, written [V = I R]. Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. To find a resistance you divide the pd by the current; multiplying them instead is the commonest error in this topic.

Resistance, R, is measured in ohms, Ω. One ohm is the resistance of a component that has a pd of one volt across it when a current of one ampere passes through it, which follows directly from R = V ÷ I.

Circuit diagrams are used to set up and check appropriate circuits to investigate the factors affecting the resistance of electrical circuits. The standard arrangement puts an ammeter in the loop with the test component and a voltmeter across it; the resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The two factors investigated are the length of a wire at constant temperature, and combinations of resistors in series and parallel.

concepts.term: Resistance and the length of a wire
concepts.definition: For a wire at constant temperature, resistance is directly proportional to length: doubling the length doubles the resistance, and a graph of resistance against length is a straight line through the origin. The temperature must be held constant, which is why the current is kept small and the circuit is switched off between readings — a wire that warms up has a higher resistance, which would spoil the pattern.

concepts.term: Resistors in series and in parallel
concepts.definition: Resistors joined in series have a combined resistance larger than either one alone, because the charge must pass through both. Resistors joined in parallel have a combined resistance smaller than either one alone, because the charge now has more than one path to take; two identical resistors in parallel give half the resistance of one.

The current through an ohmic conductor at a constant temperature is directly proportional to the potential difference across the resistor, which means that the resistance remains constant as the current changes. Its I–V graph is a straight line through the origin. A fixed resistor kept at constant temperature is the standard example.

For some resistors the value of R remains constant, but in others it can change as the current changes. The resistance of components such as lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs is not constant; it changes with the current through the component. Their I–V graphs are therefore not straight lines through the origin.

The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases. A larger current heats the filament more, so its resistance rises and its I–V graph bends over into an S-shape, becoming less steep as the pd increases. A filament lamp is therefore not an ohmic conductor.

The current through a diode flows in one direction only. The diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction, so the reverse current is very nearly zero. In the forward direction it conducts, but only once the pd is large enough, so its I–V graph lies flat along the reverse side and then rises steeply forward.

The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases. This is the opposite of the behaviour of a metal wire, whose resistance rises when it is heated, and it is what makes the thermistor useful as a temperature sensor.

In a thermostat the thermistor senses the room temperature. When the room cools, the thermistor's resistance rises; the circuit detects that change and switches the heater on. When the room warms again the resistance falls and the heater is switched off, so the temperature is held near a set value. The same idea is used in fire alarms and in engine temperature sensors.

The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light its resistance may be only a few hundred ohms; in darkness it can be millions of ohms. It is therefore used as a light sensor.

An LDR is used to switch lights on when it gets dark. As darkness falls, the light intensity on the LDR drops, so its resistance rises; the circuit senses that change and switches the street lamp on. At dawn the resistance falls again and the lamp is switched off. The same arrangement is used in automatic camera exposure and in burglar alarms.

To measure the resistance of a component, an ammeter is placed in the loop with the component so that it measures the current through it, and a voltmeter is placed across the component so that it measures the potential difference across it. The resistance is then calculated from R = V ÷ I. The circuit diagram is drawn using correct circuit symbols; a variable resistor or a variable power supply lets several pairs of readings be taken.

Graphs are used to explore whether circuit elements are linear or non-linear. A linear element gives a straight-line I–V graph through the origin and has constant resistance; a non-linear element gives a curve, and its resistance changes. The shape relates to the function of the component: the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats up, and the diode's graph is flat on one side because it conducts one way only.

Circuit diagrams are used to construct appropriate circuits to investigate the I–V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements, including a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor at constant temperature. Readings of current and pd are taken over a range of values, including reversed ones, and plotted as I against V. The resistor must be kept at constant temperature so that heating does not change the resistance being measured.

misconceptions.question: Two lamps are in series with a cell. Is the current smaller after the first lamp than before it?
misconceptions.correct: No. A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so the ammeter reads the same before, between and after the lamps.
misconceptions.misconception: The current is used up as it goes round, so there is less of it left after each lamp.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students can see the lamps glowing and know that something is being used up, and the everyday word current suggests a supply that runs out. The energy transferred by the lamps is real, so the loss is wrongly pinned on the current.
misconceptions.correction: What the lamps use is energy, not charge. Every coulomb that leaves the cell passes through both lamps and returns to it, so the current is identical at every point in the loop.

misconceptions.question: Where do the ammeter and the voltmeter go when the resistance of a component is measured?
misconceptions.correct: The ammeter goes in the loop, in series with the component; the voltmeter goes across the component, in parallel with it.
misconceptions.misconception: The voltmeter goes in the loop with the component and the ammeter goes across it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are meters that look alike on a diagram, and students remember that one goes in and one goes across without a reason to attach to each. Nothing in the two names tells them which is which.
misconceptions.correction: A voltmeter compares the potential at the two ends of a component, so it must be connected to both ends — across it. An ammeter counts the charge passing through, so the charge must go through it — in the loop.

misconceptions.question: A resistor is swapped for one of larger resistance. Does the current change?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. For the same pd, a larger resistance gives a smaller current, because resistance opposes the flow of charge.
misconceptions.misconception: A cell always pushes out the same current, so changing the component cannot change it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cells are labelled with a fixed number of volts, and students transfer that fixedness to the current, treating the cell as a pump that delivers a set amount whatever it is connected to.
misconceptions.correction: The number on a cell is its potential difference, not its current. The current is decided by the pd and the resistance together: I = V ÷ R.

misconceptions.question: A current of 0.40 A flows for 5.0 minutes. What goes into Q = I t?
misconceptions.correct: The time must be converted to seconds first: 5.0 minutes is 300 s, so Q = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C.
misconceptions.misconception: You mishandle the minutes-to-seconds conversion: substituting the time as given, so Q = 0.40 × 5.0 = 2 C, or using just 60 s, so Q = 0.40 × 60 = 24 C
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation does not visibly contain a unit, so students treat t as just a number. In most other calculations the numbers given are used exactly as they are printed.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines time, t, in seconds, s. The equation is only true with that unit, so minutes must be multiplied by 60 and hours by 3600 before substituting.

misconceptions.question: What exactly is flowing when there is a current in a wire?
misconceptions.correct: Electrical charge. The size of the current is the rate of flow of that charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Current is the flow of energy round the circuit, or it is how fast the electrons are moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Circuits are taught alongside energy transfer, so current and energy get merged. And rate of flow does sound like a speed, so the electrons' speed is substituted for the amount of charge passing each second.
misconceptions.correction: Current is charge per second, not joules per second and not metres per second. Electrons drift at well under a millimetre per second even when the current is several amperes.

misconceptions.question: Is a filament lamp an ohmic conductor?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its resistance increases as the filament gets hotter, so the current is not directly proportional to the pd and its I–V graph curves.
misconceptions.misconception: A filament lamp is ohmic, because its I–V graph passes through the origin and the current still rises when the pd rises.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students take through the origin as the whole test and stop there, or they take rising together to mean directly proportional. A curve that rises does look like agreement with the rule.
misconceptions.correction: Directly proportional means a straight line through the origin, so that equal increases in pd give equal increases in current. The lamp's line bends over, so its resistance is not constant.

misconceptions.question: A thermistor is warmed. What happens to its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases. The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating anything raises its resistance, so a hot thermistor has a higher resistance than a cold one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule met first is the metal wire one — hot filament, higher resistance — and it is generalised to every component. The thermistor is the exception, and exceptions are easily overwritten.
misconceptions.correction: A thermistor is a semiconductor, not a metal. Heating it frees more charge carriers, so its resistance drops. That opposite behaviour is exactly what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.

misconceptions.question: Bright light shines on an LDR. What happens to its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It decreases. The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.
misconceptions.misconception: More light means more for the LDR to resist, so brighter light raises its resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name light-dependent resistor is read as light causes resistance, and more of a cause is expected to give more of an effect.
misconceptions.correction: Light energy frees charge carriers inside the LDR, so more light makes it a better conductor, not a worse one. In darkness its resistance is highest, often millions of ohms.

misconceptions.question: What current passes through a diode connected the wrong way round?
misconceptions.correct: Very nearly none, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
misconceptions.misconception: A diode lets a smaller current through backwards, and has no resistance at all in the forward direction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diodes are described as one-way, which students soften into mostly one way, and the forward direction is then imagined as a perfectly free path.
misconceptions.correction: In reverse the resistance is so high that the current is effectively zero. In the forward direction the diode does have resistance, and needs a pd of a few tenths of a volt before it conducts at all.

misconceptions.question: The length of the test wire is doubled at constant temperature. What happens to its resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles. At constant temperature the resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer wire gives the charge more room to move, so a longer wire has a smaller resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Length is confused with thickness. Students correctly know that a wider wire has less resistance, and more room sounds like the same idea.
misconceptions.correction: A longer wire means more metal for the charge to push through, so more collisions and more resistance. It is a wider cross-section, not a greater length, that lowers resistance.

misconceptions.question: A second identical resistor is added in parallel. What happens to the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: It halves. Adding a resistor in parallel gives the charge another route, so the combined resistance falls.
misconceptions.misconception: Two resistors must resist more than one, so adding any extra resistor raises the total resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series case is met first and then generalised. The word resistor sounds like something that can only ever add opposition to the circuit.
misconceptions.correction: In series the charge must pass through both, so the resistances add. In parallel the charge divides between two paths, so the combined resistance is smaller than either resistor on its own.

misconceptions.question: Is the resistance of a component always the same number?
misconceptions.correct: No. For some resistors R remains constant, but in others it changes as the current changes.
misconceptions.misconception: Resistance is a fixed property of a component, like its mass, so it never changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resistance is first met as a value printed on a resistor, and printed values feel permanent. Fixed resistor is often shortened to resistor, which hides the distinction.
misconceptions.correction: Resistance is fixed only for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature. For lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs it changes with the current, and with temperature or light level.

misconceptions.question: Two I–V lines are drawn on the same axes. Which component has the greater resistance?
misconceptions.correct: The one with the shallower line. A steep line means a large current for a small pd, so a small resistance.
misconceptions.misconception: The steeper the I–V graph, the greater the resistance, because a steep graph means a big value.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Steeper is read as more of whatever the graph is about, and students do not check which quantity is on which axis before deciding.
misconceptions.correction: On I–V axes the gradient is I ÷ V, which is 1 ÷ R. A steeper line therefore means less resistance, not more.

misconceptions.question: Does potential difference flow through a component?
misconceptions.correct: No. Current flows through a component; potential difference is across it, between its two ends.
misconceptions.misconception: Potential difference flows through a component in the same way that current does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are talked about in the same sentence, and everyday talk about electricity flowing covers both words. The voltmeter is also read as measuring something inside the wire.
misconceptions.correction: Potential difference is a difference between two points, so it needs two ends to be measured between; that is why a voltmeter is connected across a component and an ammeter in the loop.

misconceptions.question: A pd of 6.0 V drives a current of 0.25 A. How is the resistance found?
misconceptions.correct: By dividing: R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.25 = 24 Ω.
misconceptions.misconception: When rearranging a formula such as V = I R or Q = I t to find the unknown, the student applies the wrong operation - multiplying instead of dividing, dividing the wrong way round, adding or subtracting the quantities, or slipping a power of ten.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is memorised as V = I R, a multiplication, and the multiplication sign is then carried over into every rearrangement of it.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I and I = V ÷ R. Only the subject of the original equation is a product; the other two are quotients.

misconceptions.question: A thermostat uses a thermistor. What happens as the room gets colder?
misconceptions.correct: The thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit responds by switching the heater on.
misconceptions.misconception: When the room gets cold the thermistor's resistance falls, letting a bigger current switch the heater on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason backwards from the outcome: the heater comes on, so something must increase, and a bigger current feels like the obvious cause.
misconceptions.correction: Cold means high resistance for a thermistor, since its resistance falls as temperature rises. It is that rise in resistance, detected as a change in pd across the thermistor, that the switching circuit responds to.

misconceptions.question: An LDR switches a street lamp on at dusk. What happens to the LDR as it gets dark?
misconceptions.correct: Its resistance rises, because an LDR's resistance falls only as light intensity increases.
misconceptions.misconception: As it gets dark the LDR's resistance falls, and that is what turns the street lamp on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The same backwards reasoning as with the thermostat: the lamp switching on is associated with something increasing, so a falling resistance and a rising current are assumed.
misconceptions.correction: Darkness means less light, so the LDR's resistance is high, not low. The switching circuit reacts to that high resistance and to the pd it produces.

misconceptions.question: Which component is drawn as a rectangle with an arrow across it?
misconceptions.correct: A variable resistor: the resistor rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it.
misconceptions.misconception: A rectangle with an arrow across it is a thermistor, or an LDR — anything whose resistance can change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Several symbols are built on the resistor rectangle, so students group them by meaning rather than by the marking that actually distinguishes them.
misconceptions.correction: The arrow across the rectangle means the resistance can be set by hand. A thermistor has a line bent at right angles; an LDR is a rectangle inside a circle with arrows pointing in at it.

misconceptions.question: Why does the resistance practical say at constant temperature?
misconceptions.correct: Because a wire that warms up has a higher resistance, which would hide the effect of length that is being investigated.
misconceptions.misconception: It only saves the battery — the wire's temperature makes no difference to the resistance measured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature effects are invisible in a short experiment, and the wire never feels hot, so the instruction looks like a safety or housekeeping rule.
misconceptions.correction: The resistance of a metal wire rises measurably when it warms, so a heating wire would give a resistance-against-length line that bends. Keeping the current small and switching off between readings holds the temperature steady.

misconceptions.question: How are the reverse readings for a diode obtained in the I–V practical?
misconceptions.correct: By turning the diode round in the circuit, or by reversing the supply connections, so that the pd is applied the other way.
misconceptions.misconception: You swap the ammeter and the voltmeter round, and that gives you the reverse readings.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reverse is attached to the meters, the most obviously reversible things on the bench, rather than to the direction of the pd across the component.
misconceptions.correction: Reversing means reversing the direction of the pd across the component. Swapping the meters would simply produce a wrong circuit, with the ammeter shorting out the component.

misconceptions.question: A closed loop of wire contains no cell. Is there a current in it?
misconceptions.correct: No. For charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: A complete loop is enough on its own — the charges are already in the metal, so they will go round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule most often repeated is that the circuit must be complete, and students take that necessary condition to be sufficient on its own.
misconceptions.correction: The free electrons are indeed already there, but they move at random in all directions. A source of pd is needed to give them a net drift in one direction, which is what a current is.

misconceptions.question: Are charge and current the same thing?
misconceptions.correct: No. Charge, Q, is measured in coulombs, C; current, I, is the rate of flow of charge and is measured in amperes, A.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge and current are the same thing, so coulombs and amperes are two names for one unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both words appear in the same definition sentence, and both are met through the same equipment, so the distinction between an amount and a rate is lost.
misconceptions.correction: The coulomb is an amount of charge, like a distance; the ampere is a rate, like a speed. One ampere is one coulomb passing each second, which is why Q = I t.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter where in a series loop the ammeter is placed?
misconceptions.correct: No. A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so any position in that loop gives the same reading.
misconceptions.misconception: An ammeter nearer the cell reads a bigger current than one further round the loop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Current is pictured as something poured out by the cell and gradually thinning as it travels, so distance from the cell is expected to matter.
misconceptions.correction: Charge cannot pile up or disappear in a wire, so the same number of coulombs passes every point each second. The ammeter can go anywhere in the loop.

misconceptions.question: Two resistors of different values are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: The two resistances add, so the total is their sum and is larger than either resistor on its own.
misconceptions.misconception: The total resistance is the average of the two resistance values, so it lies between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Faced with two numbers and unsure how to combine them, students fall back on averaging, the operation they most often use to combine values; it also gives an answer that sits comfortably between the two, which feels reasonable.
misconceptions.correction: Resistors in series are joined end to end, so the charge must pass through both and their resistances add. The total is always larger than either one, never a value between them.

misconceptions.question: A small and a large resistor are connected in series. What decides the total resistance?
misconceptions.correct: Both do: the resistances add, so the total is the sum of the two and is larger than either alone.
misconceptions.misconception: The larger resistor sets the total resistance, because it is the main obstacle to the current and the small one hardly matters.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the biggest resistor as a bottleneck that governs the whole circuit, by analogy with a chain being only as strong as its weakest link, so the smaller resistor is treated as negligible.
misconceptions.correction: In series the charge meets both resistors one after the other, so each adds its full share; the total is the sum, 3.0 Ω + 6.0 Ω = 9.0 Ω, not just the larger value.

misconceptions.question: A student wants to measure both the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Should both meters be connected across the lamp?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the voltmeter goes across (in parallel with) the lamp. The ammeter must go in the loop, in series with the lamp, so that the current being measured passes through it.
misconceptions.misconception: A meter measures a component just by being connected to it, so both the ammeter and the voltmeter are drawn across the lamp, in parallel with it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday measuring devices, like a thermometer, are simply put in contact with the thing being measured, and the voltmeter's 'across the component' rule is generalised to all meters. The idea that an ammeter must carry the very current it reads is never formed.
misconceptions.correction: An ammeter counts the charge flowing per second, so that flow must pass through it: it goes in series, in the loop with the lamp. A voltmeter compares the potential at the lamp's two terminals, so it goes in parallel, across the lamp. An ammeter placed in parallel would short-circuit the lamp because of its very low resistance.

misconceptions.question: A 3.0 ohm resistor and a 6.0 ohm resistor are joined one after the other in a single loop. A student calculates the total resistance using 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 and gets 2.0 ohm. What has gone wrong?
misconceptions.correct: The resistors are in series, so their resistances simply add: R = 3.0 + 6.0 = 9.0 ohm. The reciprocal formula is only for resistors in parallel, on separate branches between the same two points.
misconceptions.misconception: Two resistors in a circuit give the charge two routes to take, so the combined resistance is found with the parallel formula 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The series and parallel rules are memorised as two rival formulas without a picture of the circuit. 'Two resistors' cues the more distinctive reciprocal formula, and each extra component is wrongly counted as an extra path for the charge.
misconceptions.correction: Count the paths, not the components. In series there is one path: every coulomb must pass through both resistors in turn, so the oppositions accumulate and R_total = R1 + R2 = 9.0 ohm. Only when the resistors sit on separate branches between the same two points does the charge divide, and only then does 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 apply, giving a total smaller than either resistor.

mcqs.stem: A circuit diagram shows a component drawn as a plain rectangle with an arrow across it at an angle. Which component is it?

options.text: a variable resistor, whose resistance is set by hand by moving a slider
options.rationale: The standard symbol for a variable resistor is the resistor rectangle with an arrow drawn diagonally across it, showing a resistance that can be adjusted.

options.text: an LDR, whose resistance falls when the light shining on it brightens
options.rationale: Another component built on the resistor rectangle, so it attracts the same guess; the LDR symbol is a rectangle in a circle with two arrows pointing in at it.

options.text: a thermistor, whose resistance changes when its temperature alters
options.rationale: Students who know that several symbols share the rectangle pick the temperature one; the thermistor symbol carries a line bent at right angles, not an arrow.

options.text: a diode, which allows a current through it in one direction only
options.rationale: The arrow tempts students who recall an arrowhead in the diode symbol, but that symbol is a solid triangle against a line, not a rectangle.

mcqs.stem: A student is drawing a circuit diagram to measure the current through a lamp and the potential difference across it. Where should the two meters be drawn?

options.text: the voltmeter in the loop with the lamp, and the ammeter across it
options.rationale: The exact swap that many students make, because both meters look alike on a diagram and neither name says which way round it goes.

options.text: the ammeter in the loop with the lamp and the voltmeter across it
options.rationale: The charge to be counted must pass through the ammeter, so it goes in series; the voltmeter compares the potential at the lamp's two ends, so it goes across it.

options.text: both meters drawn in the loop, one on each side of the lamp
options.rationale: Chosen by students who remember that meters go in the circuit but not that a voltmeter needs both ends of a component to compare.

options.text: both meters drawn across the lamp, in parallel with each other
options.rationale: The mirror-image error; an ammeter placed across the lamp would short it out and would not measure the lamp's current at all.

mcqs.stem: A closed loop of copper wire contains no cell and no power supply. Why is there no current in it?

options.text: the free electrons in the copper drift round on their own, making a current
options.rationale: Wrong: a closed loop alone does not drive charge; a source of pd is needed for a current.

options.text: a complete copper loop needs no cell, so a current flows round it
options.rationale: Wrong: without a cell there is no pd, so no current, however complete the loop.

options.text: there is no source of potential difference to make the charge flow
options.rationale: The specification is explicit: for charge to flow through a closed circuit the circuit must include a source of potential difference.

options.text: copper has a resistance far too low for a current to be set up
options.rationale: Inverts the role of resistance: a low resistance would allow a large current, not prevent one.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the size of the electric current in a wire?

options.text: the total charge that has flowed since the circuit was switched on
options.rationale: Describes an amount of charge in coulombs rather than a rate; this is Q, not I.

options.text: the speed at which the individual electrons drift along the wire
options.rationale: Rate of flow sounds like a speed, but the drift speed is under a millimetre per second even when the current is amperes.

options.text: the energy that the cell transfers to the wire in each second
options.rationale: That quantity is power, measured in watts; current is charge per second, not joules per second.

options.text: the rate of flow of electrical charge past a given point in the wire
options.rationale: The specification defines the size of the electric current as the rate of flow of electrical charge, that is, the charge passing a point each second.

mcqs.stem: A current of 0.40 A passes through a lamp for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the charge flow.

options.rationale: Q = I t with the time converted to seconds: 5.0 minutes is 300 s, so Q = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C.
Comes from dividing the current by the time, I ÷ t, instead of multiplying them.
Uses 60 s instead of 300 s, converting only one of the five minutes.

options.text: 2 C
options.rationale: The time has been left in minutes: 0.40 × 5.0 = 2, ignoring that t must be in seconds.

mcqs.stem: In the equation Q = I t, which set of units is correct for the three quantities?

options.text: charge flow in amperes, current in coulombs, and time in seconds
options.rationale: The two electrical units have been swapped; the coulomb is an amount of charge and the ampere is a rate of flow.

options.text: charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes, time in seconds
options.rationale: Exactly as the specification gives them: charge flow, Q, in coulombs, C; current, I, in amperes, A; time, t, in seconds, s.

options.text: charge flow in coulombs, current in amperes and time in minutes
options.rationale: The electrical units are right but the time is not: the specification defines t in seconds, s.

options.text: charge flow in coulombs, current in coulombs, time in seconds
options.rationale: Wrong: current is measured in amperes and charge in coulombs; they are different quantities.

mcqs.stem: Two identical lamps are in series with a cell. An ammeter between the cell and the first lamp reads 0.30 A. It is then moved to a position between the two lamps. What does it read now?

options.text: less than 0.30 A, because the first lamp has used up some current
options.rationale: The classic used-up model; the lamps use energy, not charge, so no current is lost inside them.

options.text: less than 0.30 A, because the meter is now further from the cell
options.rationale: Wrong: current is the same everywhere in a series loop; meter position does not change it.

options.text: 0.30 A, because a current has the same value everywhere in one loop
options.rationale: A current has the same value at any point in a single closed loop, so moving the ammeter within that loop cannot change its reading.

options.text: more than 0.30 A, because it is now nearer the second lamp
options.rationale: Assumes the reading depends on position in the loop, which is precisely what the same-value rule denies.

mcqs.stem: A resistor in a circuit is replaced by one of greater resistance, and the potential difference across it is unchanged. What happens to the current through it?

options.text: it stays the same, because the cell always pushes out the same current
options.rationale: Treats the cell as a fixed source of current; the number on a cell is its pd, and the current depends on the resistance too.

options.text: it stays the same, because the pd across the component is unchanged
options.rationale: Takes the pd as the only thing that sets the current; the specification says the current depends on both the pd and the resistance.

options.text: it stays the same, because the cell alone decides the current
options.rationale: Wrong: for fixed pd, greater resistance gives a smaller current (I = V / R).

options.text: it decreases, because a greater resistance opposes the flow of charge
options.rationale: The greater the resistance of the component, the smaller the current for a given pd across it, which is I = V ÷ R.

mcqs.stem: A potential difference of 6.0 V across a component produces a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate the resistance of the component.

options.rationale: Rearranging V = I R gives R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.25 = 24 Ω, with resistance in ohms, Ω.
The division has been done upside down, I ÷ V rather than V ÷ I.
Subtracts the current from the pd; a student unsure of the rearrangement falls back on whichever operation looks easiest.
Multiplies V by I, carrying the multiplication in V = I R straight into the rearrangement.

mcqs.stem: A resistor of resistance 15 Ω has a potential difference of 3.0 V across it. Calculate the current through the resistor.

options.rationale: A place-value slip in the division, giving an answer ten times too small.
Rearranging V = I R gives I = V ÷ R = 3.0 ÷ 15 = 0.20 A, with current in amperes, A.
Divides the resistance by the pd, 15 ÷ 3.0, instead of the pd by the resistance.
Multiplies 3.0 by 15, using V = I R without rearranging it to make I the subject.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student doubles the length of nichrome wire in the circuit while keeping its temperature constant. What happens to the resistance of the wire?

options.text: it halves, because a longer wire gives the charge more room to move in
options.rationale: Confuses length with cross-section; a wider wire does have less resistance, but a longer one has more.

options.text: it is unchanged, since resistance depends only on the metal in use
options.rationale: Treats resistance as a fixed property of the material; the practical exists precisely because length changes it.

options.text: it doubles, because resistance is proportional to the wire length
options.rationale: At constant temperature the resistance of a wire is directly proportional to its length, so twice the length gives twice the resistance.

options.text: it falls to a quarter, because the longer wire gives even more room
options.rationale: Wrong: resistance is proportional to length, so doubling the length doubles the resistance.

mcqs.stem: A second resistor, identical to the first, is connected in parallel with it. What happens to the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it doubles, because two resistors must resist more than one of them
options.rationale: Applies the series rule to a parallel circuit, which is the commonest error in this practical.

options.text: it stays the same, since both resistors have the same resistance
options.rationale: Identical values are mistaken for no change; the combination is a new circuit with a lower resistance.

options.text: it doubles, because the length of resistance wire has doubled
options.rationale: Borrows the length rule from the wire experiment; in parallel the two lengths sit side by side, not end to end.

options.text: it halves, because the charge now has two separate paths to flow along
options.rationale: A parallel branch gives the charge an extra route, so the combined resistance is smaller than either resistor alone — here exactly half.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 3 a student wants to find the resistance of a length of wire. Which pair of measurements is needed?

options.text: the pd across the wire and the current in it
options.rationale: The ammeter gives I and the voltmeter gives V, and the resistance follows from R = V ÷ I.

options.text: readings from a voltmeter in the loop and an ammeter
options.rationale: These are the quantities in Q = I t; together they give the charge flow, not the resistance.

options.text: the pd across the wire and the charge that flows in it
options.rationale: This pair gives the current, which is only half of what R = V ÷ I needs.

options.text: the pd across the wire and the length of the wire
options.rationale: Length is the variable being changed, not a measurement that gives resistance; the current is still missing.

mcqs.stem: In the resistance practical, why is the voltmeter connected across the test wire rather than in the loop with it?

options.text: because a voltmeter in the loop would read the current in it instead
options.rationale: Assumes a meter measures whatever it is connected to; a voltmeter in the loop simply blocks it, because its resistance is very high.

options.text: because it must compare the potentials at the two ends of the wire
options.rationale: Potential difference is a difference between two points, so the meter must be connected to both ends of the component — across it.

options.text: because a voltmeter, like the ammeter, belongs in the loop
options.rationale: Wrong: a voltmeter must be in parallel to compare the potentials at the two ends.

options.text: because pd flows through it, so the voltmeter sits in the loop
options.rationale: Wrong: pd is measured across a component, so the voltmeter is in parallel, not in the loop.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the resistance of circuit components is correct?

options.text: R is a fixed property of every component, in the way that mass is fixed
options.rationale: True only for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature; lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs all change resistance.

options.text: R never changes, not even in a thermistor or an LDR
options.rationale: Wrong: a thermistor's and an LDR's resistance change with temperature and light.

options.text: for some components R is constant, in others it changes with current
options.rationale: Exactly the distinction the specification draws: the value of R remains constant for some resistors but can change as the current changes in others.

options.text: R only changes in components built to sense their surroundings
options.rationale: A filament lamp is not a sensor, yet its resistance rises as it heats, so sensing is not the boundary.

mcqs.stem: The I–V graph for a resistor at constant temperature is a straight line passing through the origin. What does this show?

options.text: the resistance rises steadily as the potential difference is increased
options.rationale: Reads a rising line as a rising resistance; the rising quantity is the current, while V ÷ I stays the same.

options.text: the resistance is equal to the gradient of the line at every point
options.rationale: On I–V axes the gradient is I ÷ V, which is 1 ÷ R, so the gradient is the reciprocal of the resistance.

options.text: the current does not depend on the resistor, since the cell fixes it
options.rationale: Wrong: a line through the origin shows I proportional to V, so current rises with pd.

options.text: the current is directly proportional to the pd, so the resistance is constant
options.rationale: A straight line through the origin is what direct proportionality looks like, and it means R remains constant as the current changes.

mcqs.stem: As the current through a filament lamp increases, what happens to the resistance of the lamp, and why?

options.text: it increases, because the filament becomes hotter
options.rationale: The resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases, and a larger current heats it more.

options.text: it stays constant, because the lamp is an ohmic conductor
options.rationale: A filament lamp is the standard non-ohmic example; its I–V graph curves rather than staying straight.

options.text: it stays constant, because its I–V graph passes through the origin
options.rationale: Wrong: a filament lamp is non-ohmic; its resistance rises as the filament heats up.

options.text: it increases, because a bigger current always raises resistance
options.rationale: Right direction, wrong reason: resistance rises because the metal filament gets hotter, not as a universal rule.

mcqs.stem: A diode is connected into a circuit the reverse way round. What is the current through it?

options.text: a tiny current, because the diode still leaks a little in reverse
options.rationale: Wrong: reverse current is negligible because the diode's reverse resistance is extremely high.

options.text: almost zero, because the diode has a very high resistance in reverse
options.rationale: The current through a diode flows in one direction only, because the diode has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.

options.text: much smaller than the forward current, but still easy to measure
options.rationale: Softens one-way into mostly one way; the reverse resistance is so high that the current is effectively nothing.

options.text: the same size as before, but now flowing the other way round
options.rationale: Treats the diode as an ordinary resistor that does not care about direction, which is the one thing a diode does care about.

mcqs.stem: A thermistor is taken out of a beaker of iced water and placed in a beaker of hot water. What happens to its resistance?

options.text: it increases, because heating any conductor raises its resistance
options.rationale: Generalises the metal wire rule; a thermistor is a semiconductor and behaves the opposite way.

options.text: it stays the same, because resistance depends on the material only
options.rationale: Treats resistance as a fixed property; the thermistor is listed by the specification as a component whose R is not constant.

options.text: it decreases, since a thermistor's resistance falls as it warms
options.rationale: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases, which is what makes it useful as a temperature sensor.

options.text: it increases, because the warmer thermistor resists the current more
options.rationale: Wrong: a thermistor is a semiconductor; its resistance falls as it warms.

mcqs.stem: A thermistor is used in a thermostat that switches a heater on when a room becomes too cold. What happens in the circuit as the room cools?

options.text: the thermistor's resistance falls, letting a larger current switch it on
options.rationale: Reasons backwards from the heater coming on to something increasing; a cold thermistor has a high resistance, not a low one.

options.text: the thermistor's resistance falls, so the heater stays switched off
options.rationale: Wrong: when cold the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit switches the heater on.

options.text: the thermistor's resistance is unchanged, but the pd across it rises
options.rationale: Nothing would make the pd change on its own; it is the change in resistance that redistributes the pd.

options.text: the thermistor's resistance rises, and the circuit then switches the heater on
options.rationale: Resistance falls as temperature rises, so cooling raises it; the switching circuit responds to that rise by turning the heater on.

mcqs.stem: The light shining on an LDR is made brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?

options.text: it decreases as the light on it gets brighter
options.rationale: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases, from millions of ohms in the dark to a few hundred in bright light.

options.text: it increases, as there is more light for it to resist
options.rationale: Reads the name as light causes resistance; in fact light frees charge carriers and makes the LDR conduct better.

options.text: it stays constant whatever the light level may be
options.rationale: Would make the LDR useless as a sensor; the specification lists it among components whose resistance is not constant.

options.text: it rises steadily as the light on it grows brighter
options.rationale: Wrong: an LDR's resistance falls as the light on it gets brighter.

mcqs.stem: An LDR is part of a circuit that switches a street lamp on when it gets dark. What happens as darkness falls?

options.text: the LDR's resistance falls, so a bigger current can switch the lamp on
options.rationale: Reasons backwards from the lamp lighting; resistance falls only as light increases, so darkness raises it.

options.text: the LDR's resistance rises, and so the circuit switches the lamp on
options.rationale: Less light means a higher LDR resistance, and the switching circuit responds to that change by turning the street lamp on.

options.text: the LDR's resistance falls, so the lamp is kept switched off
options.rationale: Wrong: as it darkens the LDR's resistance rises, and the circuit switches the lamp on.

options.text: the LDR's resistance does not change, but the pd across it falls
options.rationale: The pd across the LDR changes only because its resistance changes, so this leaves the sensing unexplained.

mcqs.stem: Which circuit would let a student measure the resistance of a fixed resistor?

options.text: a voltmeter in the loop with an ammeter across the resistor
options.rationale: Both meters are the wrong way round; the ammeter across the resistor would short it out entirely.

options.text: an ammeter and a voltmeter both in the loop with the resistor
options.rationale: The voltmeter's very high resistance in the loop would cut the current down to nearly nothing.

options.text: an ammeter in the loop and a voltmeter across the resistor
options.rationale: The ammeter gives the current through the component and the voltmeter the pd across it, so R = V ÷ I can be calculated.

options.text: a voltmeter across the cell with an ammeter across the resistor
options.rationale: Measures the cell rather than the component, and puts the ammeter where it cannot read the resistor's current.

mcqs.stem: A student plots I–V graphs for a fixed resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. What do the two shapes tell her?

options.text: the resistor has the greater resistance, because its line is the steeper
options.rationale: Wrong: on an I–V graph a steeper line means smaller resistance; the resistor's R is lower and constant.

options.text: both elements are linear, because in each of them the current rises as the pd rises
options.rationale: Rising together is not the same as proportional; linear requires equal increases in pd to give equal increases in current.

options.text: the lamp is linear with constant R, while the resistor's R falls as the current rises
options.rationale: Reverses both components; the resistor at constant temperature is the one with unchanging resistance.

options.text: the resistor is a linear element of constant R, while the lamp is non-linear and its R rises
options.rationale: A straight line through the origin means constant resistance; the lamp's curve flattens because the filament heats and its resistance rises.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical activity 4 the resistor must be kept at a constant temperature. Why does this matter?

options.text: so that any change of resistance from heating cannot spoil the results
options.rationale: The point of the investigation is the resistor's ohmic behaviour, which appears only if its temperature, and so its resistance, is held steady.

options.text: so that the resistor does not become hot enough to be dangerous to touch
options.rationale: Reads the instruction as a safety rule; the physics reason is that a warmer resistor has a higher resistance.

options.text: so that the cell is not drained by the current passing through the wire
options.rationale: Treats it as housekeeping for the battery; the readings would be affected even with a fresh supply.

options.text: so that the ammeter and voltmeter readings are taken at the same time
options.rationale: Confuses a good procedure with the reason for temperature control; simultaneity matters, but that is not what this instruction is for.

mcqs.stem: A charge flow of 720 C passes through a component in 3.0 minutes. Calculate the current.

options.rationale: The division has been done the wrong way round, t ÷ Q instead of Q ÷ t.

options.text: 4 A
options.rationale: I = Q ÷ t with t in seconds: 3.0 minutes is 180 s, so I = 720 ÷ 180 = 4 A.
Multiplies 720 by 3.0, using Q = I t without rearranging it to make I the subject.
Divides by 3.0 rather than by 180 s, leaving the time in minutes.

mcqs.stem: A current of 0.50 A passes through a 12 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.

options.rationale: Divides the current by the resistance, when V = I R calls for a multiplication.
Adds the two values instead of multiplying them, a fallback when the equation is only half remembered.
V = I R = 0.50 × 12 = 6.0 V, with potential difference in volts, V.
Divides the resistance by the current, 12 ÷ 0.50, rather than multiplying them.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches the I–V graph of a filament lamp?

options.text: a straight line through the origin, in both directions
options.rationale: That is the ohmic conductor's graph; the lamp is not ohmic, because its filament heats up.

options.text: a straight line whose gradient rises with the pd
options.rationale: A line cannot be straight and change gradient, and a rising gradient would mean a falling resistance.

options.text: a curve that becomes steeper as the pd is increased
options.rationale: The curve bends the other way: as the lamp heats, equal increases in pd give smaller increases in current.

options.text: an S-shaped curve that flattens as the pd rises
options.rationale: The lamp's resistance rises as the filament heats, so the graph bends over and becomes less steep in both directions.

mcqs.stem: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it is 2.0 Ω, because the charge now divides between two paths
options.rationale: This is the parallel result for 3.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω; the student has applied the parallel rule, where extra paths lower the resistance, to a series circuit, where the charge has only one path.

options.text: it is 9.0 Ω, because series resistances add together
options.rationale: Resistors in series are joined end to end, so the charge passes through both and their resistances add: 3.0 Ω + 6.0 Ω = 9.0 Ω, which is larger than either resistor alone.

options.text: it is 6.0 Ω, set by the larger of the two resistors
options.rationale: Taking the larger resistor as the one that fixes the total ignores the smaller one; in series every resistor adds its full share, so the 3.0 Ω cannot be dropped.

options.text: it is 4.5 Ω, the average of the two resistance values
options.rationale: Averaging the two values gives 4.5 Ω, a figure that sits between them; but series resistances add rather than average, so the total must exceed both, not fall between them.
